51.text:
Opinions are divided as to whether public money should be focused on healthcare or on other priorities such as education, housing and transport. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of healthcare spending argue that good health is the foundation on which everything else depends. A sick population cannot learn, work or care for children, ageing societies need more care each year, and emergencies such as pandemics show how quickly weak health systems fail. Spending on hospitals, doctors and medicines therefore saves lives and protects the economy. A patient who waits two years for surgery, for example, may lose the ability to work and need far more care later. Delays like this are costly in both human and financial terms.

On the other hand, critics point out that governments have limited funds and many equally urgent responsibilities. Many illnesses are caused by conditions that hospitals cannot change: damp housing, poor education, pollution and poverty all damage health, so spending on housing, schools and clean air can reduce hospital visits. Families living in damp homes, for example, suffer more asthma, so better housing can reduce visits to hospital. A narrow focus on treatment therefore neglects the causes of illness, and transport and education also improve lives.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that healthcare should receive a large share of public money, because it is essential and growing in demand, but not at the expense of the housing, education and environmental measures that prevent illness in the first place.

Y tế nhận phần lớn nhưng không đánh đổi các biện pháp phòng bệnh về nhà ở, giáo dục, môi trường.

151.text:
Opinions are divided as to whether public money should be directed mainly at mental health or at physical health. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of mental health spending argue that mental illness is common but often neglected. Conditions such as depression and anxiety are hidden, carry stigma and cost society through lost work, broken relationships and, in the worst cases, suicide. Early help is far cheaper than late treatment, yet many people wait months for therapy. An employee with untreated depression, for example, may be absent from work for months and strain relationships at home. Young people are especially at risk, and good support at school can prevent problems that last for decades. For these reasons, mental health deserves a larger share of spending than it usually receives.

On the other hand, critics point out that physical illness is often more visible and immediately life-threatening. Cancer, heart disease and injuries need hospitals, equipment and trained staff at once, and their results are easier to measure. A heart patient who cannot get an operation, for instance, may die within weeks, whatever else the government spends on. Mental health also tends to improve when physical needs are met, since people who are free from pain and disease are better able to cope. Funding for physical care therefore cannot be allowed to fall.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Personally, I believe that mental and physical health are closely connected and that mental health should receive a larger share than at present, while life-saving physical care remains well funded.

291.text:
In several countries the number of births is falling while the population is ageing, and opinions differ on whether public money should go to birth rate initiatives or to healthcare. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of birth rate initiatives argue that a shrinking workforce creates serious long-term problems. With fewer young workers, there are fewer taxpayers to pay for pensions and public services, and economies may grow more slowly. Childcare support, parental leave and housing help can ease the pressure on young families who delay having children because of costs. A couple that postpones starting a family until they can afford a larger home, for example, may end up with fewer children than they wanted. If such help makes it easier to have a child, the population may stabilise over time.

On the other hand, critics point out that birth rate initiatives are expensive and their results are uncertain. People decide whether to have children for many personal reasons, and the effect of financial incentives is often small and slow. Healthcare, by contrast, benefits everyone immediately, including the growing number of older people. A healthy older population also remains active and productive for longer, which helps to offset the effects of fewer young workers. Good maternal and child health services can also help families who want children to have them safely. Investment in health therefore offers more certain returns.

To sum up, both positions have their merits; nevertheless, I believe that healthcare should take priority, because its benefits are immediate and certain, although modest family support can be added.

Lực lượng lao động co lại: ít người đóng thuế trả lương hưu và dịch vụ công; hỗ trợ chăm sóc trẻ, nghỉ thai sản, nhà ở giúp gia đình trẻ. Ví dụ cặp vợ chồng hoãn sinh con đến khi mua được nhà lớn.

Y tế được ưu tiên vì lợi ích tức thì và chắc chắn, có thể thêm hỗ trợ gia đình khiêm tốn.

373.text:
Opinions are divided as to whether public money should be spent mainly on public health campaigns or on hospital infrastructure. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of public health campaigns argue that preventing illness is cheaper and kinder than treating it. Campaigns against smoking, poor diet and infectious disease reach millions of people at a relatively low cost and can change habits that cause serious illness. Vaccination drives and health education stop disease before it starts, so fewer people ever need a hospital bed. A campaign that teaches handwashing, for example, can reduce infections in schools at very little cost. Over time, a healthier population also means lower spending on treatment and more people able to work.

On the other hand, advocates of hospital infrastructure point out that people who are already ill need treatment now. Campaigns cannot cure disease, accidents and genetic conditions cannot be prevented, and hospitals need modern buildings, equipment and staff to cope with emergencies and an ageing population. A rural hospital without a scanner, for instance, must send patients on long journeys that can delay diagnosis. Old, overcrowded facilities also put staff under pressure and increase waiting times. A health system that neglects treatment loses public trust, however good its campaigns may be.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that prevention deserves a growing share of the budget because it offers the best long-term value, while hospitals must still receive enough money to provide safe, modern care for those who need it today.

433.text:
Opinions are divided as to whether public money should be spent mainly on preventive healthcare or on treatment services. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of prevention argue that stopping illness before it develops is cheaper and kinder than curing it. Regular screening, vaccination and advice on diet, exercise and smoking identify problems early, when they are simple and inexpensive to deal with. A cancer found at an early stage, for example, may be treated with minor surgery, whereas the same disease found late may require years of costly care. Preventive measures also keep people productive and independent, and each unit of money spent on prevention can save several times as much on treatment later. Healthy habits learned in childhood can last a lifetime.

On the other hand, supporters of treatment services point out that illness cannot always be prevented. Accidents, genetic conditions and infections strike even careful people, and those who are already sick need skilled help immediately, not advice about their future. Hospitals, emergency teams and specialist doctors save lives every day, and the public rightly expects the state to provide them. A patient with a broken spine, for instance, depends on emergency treatment and long-term rehabilitation, not on prevention campaigns. Reducing treatment budgets would cause suffering and anger.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Personally, I believe that prevention should receive a larger share than it does now because it offers better long-term value, but treatment must remain well funded so that nobody is left without care.

301.text:
Ageing populations, rising costs and the lessons of recent epidemics have made health a central political issue. I firmly believe that countries should invest more in health, since healthier people are more productive and cost less in the long run, and since good health is a basic need that everyone shares.

To begin with, healthier people are more productive and cost less in the long run. A healthy workforce takes fewer sick days, works more efficiently and supports economic growth, while people who are ill or caring for sick relatives often cannot work at all. Prevention and early treatment are also much cheaper than late, emergency care. A country that funds screening and primary care, for example, may avoid expensive hospital admissions that could have been prevented. Health spending is therefore an investment that repays itself over time, rather than a pure cost.

Furthermore, strong health services make a country safer and fairer. Good hospitals, trained staff and reliable supplies allow a country to respond quickly to epidemics, which protects both lives and the economy. Access to care also gives poorer people a fair chance in life, since illness is a major cause of poverty. Admittedly, spending more on health requires higher taxes or cuts elsewhere, and money must be used efficiently to avoid waste. However, the benefits in lives saved, reduced suffering and economic strength far outweigh these costs, particularly as populations grow older.

In conclusion, I believe that countries should invest more in health, because it raises productivity, saves money in the long term and protects the most vulnerable.

80.text:
Many people suffer from depression, anxiety and other mental health problems, yet professional help is often expensive or hard to reach. I largely agree that mental health services should be free, since cost prevents many people from getting early treatment, although there are practical limits to what can be provided.

To begin with, free mental health services remove the cost barrier to early treatment. Therapy and medication are expensive, so many people go without help until their condition becomes severe, while early support keeps them working and out of hospital. A student with anxiety who can see a counsellor for free, for example, may recover quickly and finish her studies, whereas one who cannot afford help may drop out. Untreated problems also tend to get worse, which makes later care more complicated and more costly for everyone.

Furthermore, free services bring wider benefits to society. People who recover are able to work, look after their families and take part in community life, which raises productivity and reduces pressure on hospitals, welfare and even the justice system. Free access also helps to reduce stigma, because seeking help becomes a normal part of healthcare. However, there are limits. Free services cost taxpayers a great deal, demand may increase sharply, waiting lists can grow long and there is often a shortage of trained therapists. Governments may therefore need to introduce them in stages, starting with those in greatest need, and train more professionals.

In conclusion, mental health services should be free to a large extent, because this allows early treatment and benefits society, provided that governments plan carefully for staffing and demand.

5.text:
Health is often treated as a private matter, yet a country's wealth depends heavily on the wellbeing of its people. This essay will outline two principal benefits for a country that focuses on health: a stronger economy and a better quality of life.

First and foremost, a focus on health strengthens the economy. Healthier people are more productive and cost less in the long run. A healthy workforce takes fewer sick days, works more efficiently and supports economic growth, and fewer families are pushed into poverty by medical bills. Prevention and early treatment are also much cheaper than emergency care, so spending on health frees money for other uses. A country that provides vaccination and clean water, for example, spends far less on treating diseases that could have been avoided. Healthy children also learn better at school, which builds a more skilled population for the future.

In addition, a focus on health improves quality of life and social stability. People live longer and enjoy their later years in better condition, and families are spared the grief and burden of preventable illness. Strong health services also make the country safer, since they can respond quickly to epidemics and disasters. Where health care is available to everyone, people feel more secure and more equal, which supports trust in public institutions. Although providing good health services is expensive, a nation that invests in the wellbeing of its people gains a more productive, more cohesive society, and the returns continue across generations.

To sum up, focusing on health brings clear benefits to a country, above all a stronger economy and a better, more secure quality of life. For these reasons, it deserves sustained public support.
